title: Behind the Swipe: How an Application Actually Works
description: What actually happens between a swipe and the next video. Follow one action through the system, learn why events and state are different, and see where AI fits inside an application.

objectives.label: Explain how an action becomes a structured event the system can record
Explain state as what the system currently knows or believes to be true
Trace how one action travels through a loop of request, computation, and response
Explain why AI is one computation component inside an application, not the whole application

blocks.text:
You watch a short video for about three seconds, then swipe away. The next video seems to guess something about you. What did the application actually receive in those three seconds?

Common guesses say you were bored, not interested, or that the topic should stop. The phone never receives the sentence "I am bored." It cannot directly observe boredom, enjoyment, or intention.

It observes behavior. The difference between what a person means and what a system can measure is one of the core problems in product design.

blocks.alt: A simplified event record listing fields such as user, video, watch time, completion, like, share, action and timestamp
blocks.caption: A simplified classroom example, not any real application's internal record.

blocks.text:
An event is a structured record that something happened. Fields like watch_time, completed, and action: swipe_next store measurable facts, not feelings.

Nowhere in this record does it say the viewer was bored. The system must infer possible interest from the actions it can observe, and that inference can be wrong.

blocks.question: Look at the event record. Where does it say the student was bored?

options.label: In the action field, as swipe_next
Nowhere. The system must infer interest from the actions it can observe.

blocks.explanation: The record stores what happened, not what it meant. A 3.2 second watch time and a swipe_next action are evidence. Boredom is an interpretation the system would have to infer from that evidence, and it can never be certain it is right.

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: Computers do not receive intentions. They receive evidence.

lessons.title: How one swipe travels through a system

blocks.alt: A flow from a finger movement to a device event, a request to a server, computation, a response and a rendered next video
blocks.caption: Watch video, swipe, next video appears. The gap between the swipe and the next video is where the whole system lives.
steps: The application creates a swipe event
A request travels to a server
The server reads the user and session state
Computation scores and ranks candidate videos
The application renders the next video

blocks.text:
The touchscreen first measures where and how the finger moved. The application then interprets that gesture as an event such as SWIPE_NEXT. A request is a message asking another part of the system to perform work or return information.

Before choosing the next video, the server reads state: who is asking, what has already been shown, and which videos are available. Computation then validates, searches, scores, ranks, and selects. The response returns information. Rendering turns those fields into video, text, and buttons the person can use.

A feed is not simply a list of videos. It is a repeated decision. The next video is a prediction generated from previous evidence.

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: To a person, it is a swipe. To the application, it is an event.

blocks.question: A swipe sends a request across the internet. What is the internet actually doing in this loop?

options.label: Choosing which video is most likely to interest you
Carrying the request to a computer that can make the decision
Storing your account so the app can show your likes
Rendering the next video on your screen

blocks.explanation: The internet moves messages between computers. It is transportation, not intelligence. The decision about the next video happens on a server that reads state, applies rules, and scores candidates. The device then renders whatever came back.

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: The internet is transportation, not intelligence.

lessons.title: State, loops, and where AI fits

slides.title: The emoji is not the feature

blocks.text:
A messaging app streak looks like a fire emoji and a number. The emoji is only what the application renders. The real feature is stored state, plus timing rules, plus each new Snap event.

State is what the system currently knows or believes to be true: last Snap times both ways, streak days, and whether the streak is still active. The displayed emoji can leave one screen while that stored record still exists on another device.

Events are records of what happened. State is the current picture the system calculates from those events and its rules.

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: Events are what happened. State is what is true now.

blocks.title: How a streak is computed
steps: A student sends a Snap. The application creates a SEND_SNAP event with sender, recipient, and time.
The system verifies the sender and recipient, then decides whether this Snap qualifies for the streak.
It stores the timestamp and checks both directions against the daily time window.
The streak state is kept, increased, or allowed to expire from those rules.
Updated state returns. The application renders the fire, the number, or the hourglass from that calculated state.

blocks.question: A user opens the account on a second phone and sees the same streak number. What is the streak actually?

options.label: The fire emoji saved on the first phone
A stored record of events plus rules that the app calculates and renders
A notification the app sends at midnight
The count of snaps inside the last message

blocks.explanation: The emoji and number are rendered from state, so any device that reads the same account shows the same streak. The streak itself is the saved record and the timing rules, recalculated from new events. The emoji can vanish from one screen while the stored state still exists.

slides.title: Your device is not the whole game

blocks.text:
In an online game, pressing Jump does not send a video of the character to every other player. The client on your device detects the input, may show a predicted jump immediately, and sends a message describing the action to the server.

The server is the referee. It checks whether the jump is valid, updates the official shared state, and sends that state to connected players. Each device then renders the result. When the local prediction and the server disagree, the server wins and the screen snaps back.

Your device proposes an action. The server settles the argument. The screen may show what the application expects to become true before the server has confirmed it.

When an AI app answers, the screen first collects the message, conversation context, account information, and instructions. The application packages a request that often contains far more than the one visible sentence.

A server may verify identity, choose a model, retrieve saved context, and limit the request. The model then performs inference: it processes the supplied context and calculates likely next pieces of the response. The application may also search, query a database, or call other tools before it checks, stores, and renders the result.

The model does not automatically know the user. It knows the context the system provides. AI is a computation service inside a product pipeline, not the entire application.

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: Software is not a screen. Software is a loop that responds to events and changes state.
